book: 282 - Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There

chapters.relation: Hans Florine's foreword frames climbing as a way of posing philosophical questions rather than settling them, echoing the book's 'it's the journey' ethos, and previews debates the volume takes up: the sanity/morality of free soloing, hold chipping, and how routes are graded. Florine describes himself as an Ayn Rand Objectivist who also carries Buddhist concern and treats logic as a reliable tool, and calls the 100-percent focus of climbing 'physical meditation.' No taxonomy philosopher (Rand) is actually deployed in argument; the piece is a personal, agenda-setting foreword rather than a sustained application of a philosophical position.

Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.

Kevin Krein argues that the freedom climbers report feeling is not freedom of movement, political freedom, or free will—on those measures a roped climber pinned on a ledge is less free—but the Stoic freedom of aligning one's will with what nature allows. Using Chrysippus' tethered-dog image and the Stoic identification of human logos with cosmic reason, he claims the climber who understands and accepts the mountain's conditions and wills only what it permits becomes free, which is why experienced climbers feel freest when their options are fewest. He adds Epictetus' dichotomy of control: the mountain (storms, avalanches, one's own failing body) is largely outside our power, so limiting desire to what we control—composure, choices, effort—is how a climber stays free in any conditions.

Prompted by the avalanche death of his climbing partner Charlie on the Super Couloir, Paul Charlton uses Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism to ask whether the risks of climbing can be ethically justified, insisting that blindly accepting risk is indefensible but deliberate, reasoned risk can be right. He weighs climbing's costs (frivolity, self-focus, danger to self and to grieving family) against its intrinsic value (joy, friendship, aesthetic experience) and instrumental value (cultivating human excellence, psychological growth, reprioritized lives), invoking Mill's higher/lower pleasures to argue quality of happiness matters, not just quantity. His conclusion is that climbing can be justified only when it produces more overall good than any alternative use of that time, leaving each climber to run the calculation for their own case.

Joe Fitschen distinguishes justifying climbing (weak, self-revealing answers) from explaining why humans climb, and offers an evolutionary, naturalistic explanation: the ability and pleasure of climbing are inherited arboreal dispositions that were not selected out and can still have utility, so Mallory's 'because it's there' names a real, gene-rooted urge. He deploys Wittgenstein's analysis of 'game' and family resemblances to block the fallacy of universality—the fact that some people lack the urge to climb says nothing against its evolutionary roots—and warns against teleological thinking about traits. He also treats climbing's pleasures (physical, aesthetic, emotional) and its style-based ethics (bolting disputes, ego vs. the pleasure of the experience) as expressions of an evolved, social human nature.

Heidi Howkins Lockwood examines the 'asymmetry thesis'—that a climber's gratuitous risk is less acceptable than an astronaut's necessary risk—and argues its two standard defenses fail: the Rule of Rescue is neither necessary (free soloists need no rescue yet are condemned) nor sufficient (Hornbein and Unsoeld's risky Everest traverse was praised because it succeeded), and the argument from compassion collapses into circularity. She then shows the intuition is really driven by external background assumptions, especially gender inequality: the media vilified climber-mother Alison Hargreaves while lauding astronaut-mother Christa McAuliffe, because ambition-for-profit violates the 'traditionally female' role of service. She concedes a limited, defensible version tied to the assumption that seeking risk as a mere end (rather than an ineliminable means) is irresponsible.

Brian Treanor argues from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics that climbing is a crucible for cultivating virtues (arete) that contribute to flourishing (eudaimonia), stressing that virtue is acquired by habituation and lies in a mean 'relative to us'—so casting off on the Bachar-Yerian is courage for a 5.11 leader but rashness for a 5.9 climber. He shows how climbing's self-imposed 'rules' (Tejada-Flores' games) forge courage (feeling the right balance of fear and confidence, as in John Sherman's Fisher Towers epic and Steve House's judicious retreats on K7), humility (honestly measuring oneself against pioneers who used inferior gear, per Chouinard and Messner's 'murder of the impossible'), and reverence for nature (Thoreau, Muir, Brower). His thesis is that in a coddled, technological world climbing is uncommonly well suited to building these excellences of character.

Pam Sailors distinguishes two kinds of high-altitude climber: the goal-oriented 'summiteer,' who pursues the summit at all costs for self-affirmation and may neglect others, and the process-oriented 'mountaineer,' who seeks relationship with the mountain, attains self-transcendence, and feels moral responsibility for comrades. Drawing on J. S. Russell and Jonathan Simon, and on cases like the 2006 abandonment of David Sharp versus Dan Mazur giving up his summit to save Lincoln Hall, she argues both types find value in dangerous sport but that the mountaineer—exhibiting courage, compassion, and care—is the morally better person. She backs this with Reinhold Messner, Ed Viesturs, and Sherpa judgment that mountains are not conquered but simply allow, or do not allow, us to climb them.

Philip Ebert and Simon Robertson defend the self-sufficiency thesis (S): other things being equal, the more self-sufficiently a mountaineering objective is achieved, the better the achievement. Ranking Hermann Buhl's solo, free, alpine-style first ascent of Nanga Parbat above a hypothetical roped-team version and far above a guided, oxygen-and-porter Everest ascent, they argue self-sufficiency (alpine over siege, solo over team, free over aid) is good because it is more committing and adventurous and is partly constitutive of mountaineering itself. They handle objections about foolhardiness (Lafaille on Makalu), incomparable routes (Lhotse South Face), teamwork, and blind climber Erik Weihenmayer via an 'other things being equal' clause, and conclude self-sufficiency acts as a catalyst raising the subjective difficulty and thus the value of every other mountaineering good.

Ben Levey uses the fast-food (sport) versus haute-cuisine (trad) analogy and then Hegel's Phenomenology to argue that trad climbing offers a more authentic experience than sport climbing. Applying the master–slave dialectic, he casts the trad climber (like his mentor Martin risking a groundfall on 'Resurrection' placing natural protection) as the slave: through genuine fear, the setting aside of desire, and work that leaves the rock in its independent, unaltered state, the climber comes to identify with the world rather than dominate it. Sport climbing, where bolts subordinate the rock's natural features to the climber's chosen safe line, corresponds to the master who never overcomes the world's independence, yielding only the limited satisfaction of having played the game ethically.

Eric Swan argues that climbing embodies the principles and spirit of Zen, the experience of 'ordinary mind' finding the extraordinary in the ordinary and living fully in the present. Tracing Zen from the Buddha's Flower Sermon and Bodhidharma through Suzuki's 'Beginner's Mind' and Huineng's finger-and-moon, he maps Zen's four training paths—physical work, zazen (sitting meditation), koans, and interviews with masters—onto climbing: routes are like koans solved by insight and action rather than logic, 'being in the zone' is meditative absorption, and breath-regulation at the crux is zazen in motion. He holds up free soloist Derek Hersey, grinning hundreds of feet up Eldorado Canyon, and Chris Sharma, who writes of flowing 'like water' on the rock, as modern Zen masters who dissolve the separation between self, climb, and world.

holes.name: Evolutionary Explanation of Human Behavior
holes.what: The Darwinian, naturalistic strategy of explaining human traits, urges, and pleasures as inherited dispositions favored (or not selected out) by natural selection rather than by conscious purpose.
holes.why: Chapter 3 (Fitschen) is fundamentally an evolutionary explanation of why humans climb—arboreal dispositions carried forward, pleasures as adaptive—and the taxonomy has no Darwin/evolution philosopher or evolutionary-psychology concept to capture its central move.

holes.name: Philosophy of Sport (value internal to athletic activity)
holes.what: The study of values internal to games and sports—style, difficulty, self-sufficiency, adventure—by which one athletic achievement is judged better or more admirable than another.
holes.why: Chapter 7 (Ebert and Robertson) argues self-sufficiency is a good-making value partly constitutive of mountaineering itself, an internal-to-sport value theory the taxonomy has no philosopher or concept for; the same gap recurs in Sailors' 'value of dangerous sport' (ch 6).
